title: Given a `List<Employee>`, check whether any employee earns above a threshold (`anyMatch`), whether all employees are adults (`allMatch`), and whether none belong to a blocked department (`noneMatch`). Explain how these short-circuiting terminals behave and what they return for an empty stream.
shortTitle: Validate a batch of employees using anyMatch, allMatch, and noneMatch
keyPoints: `anyMatch`, `allMatch`, and `noneMatch` are short-circuiting terminal operations that take a `Predicate` and return a primitive `boolean`.
`anyMatch` is `true` if at least one element matches; it stops at the first match.
`allMatch` is `true` if every element matches; it stops at the first element that fails.
`noneMatch` is `true` if no element matches; it stops at the first element that matches.
On an empty stream, `anyMatch` is `false` while both `allMatch` and `noneMatch` are `true` (vacuously).
Short-circuiting means they rarely scan the whole stream, which makes them efficient on large data.
They answer existence and validation questions, not transformation, so they return a boolean rather than a new stream.

s1_definition.oneliner: `anyMatch` = at least one, `allMatch` = every one, `noneMatch` = not a single one; all take a `Predicate`, short-circuit, and return a boolean.
s1_definition.profdef:
Three terminal checks answer yes-or-no questions about a stream.

- **`anyMatch(predicate)`** – returns `true` the moment it finds one element that matches, otherwise `false`.
- **`allMatch(predicate)`** – returns `false` the moment it finds one element that fails, otherwise `true`.
- **`noneMatch(predicate)`** – returns `false` the moment it finds one element that matches, otherwise `true`.
- **Short-circuiting** – each stops traversing as soon as the answer is certain, so it rarely reads every element.
- **Empty-stream rule** – `anyMatch` is `false`, while `allMatch` and `noneMatch` are both `true` vacuously.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh is inspecting a batch of account-opening forms. "Is there any form over ten lakh?" – he stops the moment he finds one (`anyMatch`). "Are all the forms signed?" – he stops the moment he finds an unsigned one (`allMatch`). "Is there no form from a blocked branch?" – he stops the moment he finds a blocked one (`noneMatch`). If the tray is empty, he found no high-value form, yet trivially every form he saw was signed and none were blocked.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  anyMatch(salary > 10L)   -- stops at first MATCH

  [800k] [1200k] [990k] [1500k] ...
     │      │
     ▼      ▼
   no match │ MATCH -> return true immediately
            └──────────────► rest never checked
```

```text
  allMatch(age >= 18)      -- stops at first FAILURE

  [34] [29] [15] [41] ...
    │    │    │
    ▼    ▼    ▼
   ok   ok  FAIL -> return false immediately
             └──────────► rest never checked
```

```text
  noneMatch(dept in blocked)  -- stops at first MATCH

  [Trading] [Risk] [Sanctions] [Settlement] ...
      │       │        │
      ▼       ▼        ▼
     ok      ok      MATCH -> return false immediately
```

```text
  Empty stream results

  ┌────────────┬─────────┐
  │ anyMatch   │  false  │  nothing can match
  ├────────────┼─────────┤
  │ allMatch   │  true   │  vacuously: no element fails
  ├────────────┼─────────┤
  │ noneMatch  │  true   │  vacuously: no element matches
  └────────────┴─────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
For yes-or-no checks over a collection I use the three matching terminals: `anyMatch` is `true` if at least one element satisfies the predicate, `allMatch` is `true` if every element does, and `noneMatch` is `true` if not a single element does. All three are short-circuiting, which means they stop traversing the moment the answer is certain – `anyMatch` stops at the first match, `allMatch` stops at the first failure, and `noneMatch` stops at the first match – so they stay efficient on large data.

In my banking work at the National Bank of India I used them as a compliance gate before onboarding a batch. `anyMatch` told me whether any candidate was a very high earner needing extra approval, `allMatch` confirmed every candidate was an adult, and `noneMatch` confirmed nobody came from a sanctioned department. Each returns a clean boolean that feeds the gate decision, which reads far better than a manual loop with a flag.

The senior detail I always mention is the empty-stream behaviour, because it trips people up. On an empty stream `anyMatch` is `false`, while both `allMatch` and `noneMatch` are `true`, vacuously, because "all of nothing" and "none of nothing" are trivially satisfied. Knowing that prevents a surprising bug when a batch happens to be empty and an "all approved" check lets it slip through, so I guard emptiness explicitly when it matters.

Think of Rajesh inspecting a tray of forms: he stops at the first big form, the first unsigned form, or the first blocked form, and if the tray is empty he saw no violation at all.

Remember one sentence: `anyMatch` needs one, `allMatch` needs every one, `noneMatch` needs not a single one, and on an empty stream only `anyMatch` is `false`.
